prediction.whatIsNeededForEstimate: This value turns on facts the materials do not state: the injured person's medical expenses and lost earnings, past and future, with their amounts. Add them and run the estimate again.
prediction.likelyOutcome: Liability against Khalia on the negligent-security theory is strong given the documented prior in-store shooting just three days earlier, chronic drug/loitering activity requiring multiple daily police visits, Khalia's failure to pursue a criminal trespass warning, inadequate exterior camera coverage, and the manager's impeached trial testimony about a no-documentation policy -- which also meaningfully supports submitting punitive damages to the jury. Comparative fault exposure for Rosebud personally appears low since he was an uninvolved bystander, though Khalia will press for apportionment of fault to the non-party shooter and possibly co-tenants/landlord. The case cannot be dollar-valued on this record because no medical, wage, or prior demand/verdict figures were provided.
missingFacts: the injured person's medical expenses and lost earnings, past and future, with their amounts

outcome.description: The jury returned a verdict of $1,718,367.46 in total damages, finding Khalia 66% at fault and the driver and the shooter 17% each; the trial court entered judgment against Khalia of approximately $1.134 million (66% of the verdict is $1,134,122.52), denied JNOV and new trial, and awarded Rosebud $140,951.17 in fees and expenses under OCGA 9-11-68 after Khalia rejected his $150,000 demand (Khalia's highest offer was $50,000). The Court of Appeals affirmed on December 6, 2019.
outcome.finalNote: Affirmed. The opinion states the judgment only as approximately $1.134 million; the figure here is 66% of the stated verdict.

source.caseName: Khalia, Inc. v. Daniel Rosebud (and vice versa)

source.excerptNote: Verbatim from the statement of facts (the shooting at 490 Fairburn Road and the evidence of prior crime, security practices and cameras), with the opening clause 'Thus viewed in favor of the verdict, the record shows that' cut from the first sentence. Removed: the opening paragraph (states the demand together with the verdict amount), the standard-of-review paragraph, the directed-verdict rulings, verdict, apportionment and judgment, the post-trial motions, and all analysis, including the fee section where the parties' highest offers ($50,000 and $150,000) are recited; those offers are not in the input because every sentence stating them also states or implies the outcome. The opinion gives no medical or economic damages figures.
